course.title: A+ Capstone Bench
course.description: A used desktop arrives at the help desk with no record and a fault. Bring it back on a real bench: image it before anything changes, build and secure it, work the tickets, and hand it over documented.
course.audience: Rebuild, support and hand over one real desktop as a four-person bench team — everyone opens the case, pastes the proof and fills every record; the focus decides which record you lead.

roles.name: Hardware Bench (Bench Lead)
roles.mission: Leads the hardware record: inventory, the fault log, firmware and the physical build.

roles.name: Systems Build (Systems Lead)
roles.mission: Leads the system record: the image, the install, drivers, updates and the baseline.

roles.name: Help Desk (Support Lead)
roles.mission: Leads the ticket log: user setup, peripherals, remote help and every fault worked.

roles.name: Service Records (Records Lead)
roles.mission: Leads the records that outlive the bench: intake, backups, security and handover.

weeks.title: Preparation
weeks.objective: Set the bench up safely, gather tools and media, register the PC as received, and pick your focus.
weeks.milestone: The strap is on, the live USB boots on the bench PC, the image drive has room, and the intake record names the machine.

weeks.title: Bench
weeks.theme: What arrived, and why it does not boot
weeks.objective: Inventory the machine from a live USB, work its fault with the six-step method, and set the firmware baseline.

objectives.label: Work the fault with the method

weeks.milestone: Every part is a row with its real model, the fault is fixed with the failed theories kept, and the firmware is set and recorded.

weeks.title: Systems
weeks.objective: Image the disk before any change, install and update Windows, set accounts, and prove the image restores.

objectives.label: Image the disk before anything changes

weeks.milestone: An image with a hash exists from before the install, Windows is installed, updated and baselined, and a restore from the image was run and timed.

weeks.title: Support
weeks.objective: Connect the PC, set up the user and peripherals, then work three injected faults as tickets.

objectives.label: Connect it and prove the link
Set up the user and the peripherals
Work three tickets with the method

weeks.milestone: The PC is on the network with a standard user, a printer and remote help, and three tickets are closed with the method shown on each.

weeks.title: Hand over
weeks.theme: Secure it, prove the restore, hand it over
weeks.objective: Secure the machine, take the final image, time a real restore, and hand over the as-built with custody.

objectives.label: Take the final image and time the restore

weeks.milestone: Encryption and Defender are on and proven, the final image restores inside the target, and the as-built package carries a hashed custody row for every artifact.

tasks.title: Make the bench safe and register the machine
tasks.objective: Set the bench up so nothing is damaged, then record the PC exactly as it arrived before anyone opens it.
definitionOfDone: The strap is worn and clipped to bare metal whenever the case is open
The intake record names the machine, its condition and what came with it
A photo of the machine as received is saved and hashed

steps.title: Lay the bench out and put the strap on
steps.description: The strap is on, clipped to the chassis, and the bench holds only the PC, the tools and the media.
steps.instruction: Clear a flat, dry surface. Put the anti-static strap on your wrist and clip it to bare metal on the case. Keep drinks off the bench.
steps.expectedOutput: The strap is on, clipped to the chassis, and the bench holds only the PC, the tools and the media.
instructionList: Unplug the PC from the wall before the case comes off. The power switch on the supply is not enough.
Wear the strap and clip it to unpainted metal on the case; a strap clipped to plastic does nothing.
Keep screws in a lid or tray, grouped by where they came from.
Tick each safety line in the Intake & Bench Checklist as you do it.
steps.whatItMeans: A static discharge you cannot feel can kill a memory module. The strap costs nothing and the habit lasts a career.

steps.title: Record the machine as received
steps.description: The intake record names the machine with its tag, its condition and the accessories, and the photo is saved.
steps.instruction: Before touching anything inside, write down the make, model, service tag, what came with it and its condition. Photograph it from the front and the back.
steps.expectedOutput: The intake record names the machine with its tag, its condition and the accessories, and the photo is saved.
instructionList: Read the service tag or serial from the sticker on the case, not from memory.
List everything that came with it: power lead, keyboard, mouse, any drive or stick.
Describe the condition honestly: dents, missing covers, a rattle, a smell.
Save the photos as evidence and hash them from the Deliverables page.
steps.whatItMeans: The record of what arrived is the record you defend later if a client says a part went missing.

tasks.title: Build the live USB, the installer and the image drive
tasks.objective: Write a Linux live system and a Windows installer to USB, and prepare the external drive that will hold the images.
tools: A USB drive of at least 4 GB
definitionOfDone: The live USB boots on the bench PC to a shell
The Windows installer USB is written from media whose checksum matched
The image drive is formatted, labelled and has at least twice the PC disk free

steps.title: Check the downloads before you write them
steps.description: A checksum that matches is the only proof the image is the one the publisher made.
steps.instruction: Download the Linux live image, the Clonezilla image and the Windows installer media. Compare each checksum with the one on the download page before writing anything.
instructionList: Use the official download pages only. A mirror that offers no checksum is not a source.
Run the hash on each file and compare every character, not the first four.
Record the three hashes in the Intake & Bench Checklist.

commands.explain: The hashes of the Linux and Clonezilla images. Compare with the download page.
commands.sample:
e5f2…a1c0  ubuntu-24.04-desktop-amd64.iso
9b31…77de  clonezilla-live-3.2.0-5-amd64.iso

commands.explain: On Windows: the installer media hash, printed as one line.
commands.sample:
Algorithm       Hash
---------       ----
SHA256          36DE5ECB7A0DAA58DCE68C03B9465A543ED0F5498AA8AE60AB45FB7C8C4AE402

steps.whatItMeans: An installer that was tampered with on the way down installs the attacker along with Windows. The hash is thirty seconds of insurance.
steps.expectedOutput:
$ sha256sum ubuntu-24.04-desktop-amd64.iso
e5f2…a1c0  ubuntu-24.04-desktop-amd64.iso

PS> Get-FileHash .\Win11_24H2_English_x64.iso -Algorithm SHA256
Algorithm       Hash
---------       ----
SHA256          36DE5ECB7A0DAA58DCE68C03B9465A543ED0F5498AA8AE60AB45FB7C8C4AE402

steps.title: Write the sticks and prepare the image drive
steps.description: The live USB reaches a desktop or shell on the bench PC and the IMAGES drive mounts with room for two full…
steps.where: Your own laptop, then the bench PC
steps.instruction: Write the Linux image to one stick and the Windows installer to another. Format the external drive as IMAGES, then boot the live stick on the bench PC.
steps.expectedOutput: The live USB reaches a desktop or shell on the bench PC and the IMAGES drive mounts with room for two full images.
instructionList: Label each stick with tape: LIVE and INSTALL. A wrong stick in Week 2 wipes the wrong disk.
Boot the bench PC from LIVE: tap the boot-menu key at the logo and pick the USB entry.
Plug in IMAGES and confirm it mounts with free space of at least twice the PC disk.

fixes.symptom: The PC ignores the stick and boots to a black screen?
fixes.fix: Enter firmware setup, turn Secure Boot off for now and put USB first in the boot order. Record both changes in the firmware baseline next week.

fixes.symptom: Rufus asks about partition scheme?
fixes.fix: GPT for UEFI on any PC from the last decade. MBR only if firmware setup offers no UEFI mode.

steps.whatItMeans: Every proof in Week 1 runs from the live stick, and every image lands on the IMAGES drive. Both have to work before the clock starts.

tasks.title: Know your team, your focus and the folder
tasks.objective: Agree who leads which record, name the PC, and set up the team folder every artifact goes in.
definitionOfDone: Each of the four focuses has a named member
The PC has a hostname in the pattern BENCH-T<team>
The team folder exists with a week-0 to week-4 layout

steps.title: Pick the focus and name the machine
steps.description: Four names against four focuses, and a hostname the whole team uses from now on.
steps.instruction: Agree who leads Hardware, Systems, Help Desk and Records. Name the PC BENCH-T followed by your team number and write both into the intake record and the Lab access panel.
steps.expectedOutput: Four names against four focuses, and a hostname the whole team uses from now on.
steps.whatItMeans: A focus is the record a member leads and reviews, not the only work they do. Everyone opens the case and everyone pastes output.

steps.title: Make the team folder
steps.description: One folder on the IMAGES drive, one subfolder per week, so every artifact has one home.
steps.instruction: Create the team folder on the IMAGES drive with a subfolder for each week. Every screenshot, log and image goes under the week it belongs to.

commands.explain: Five week folders in one command. Replace t1 with your team number.
Read it back. Five folders, nothing else.
commands.sample: week-0  week-1  week-2  week-3  week-4

steps.whatItMeans: An artifact nobody can find is an artifact nobody can hash. The folder is the first custody control.
steps.expectedOutput:
$ ls /media/$USER/IMAGES/bench-t1/
week-0  week-1  week-2  week-3  week-4

tasks.title: Read what is really inside
tasks.objective: Open the case and list every part by what it is, then prove each one from the live system rather than the sticker.
definitionOfDone: Every part is a row: board, CPU, memory per slot, storage, supply, cards, ports
Each row carries the model the live system reported, not the one on the box
The disk health is recorded with the line that says so

steps.title: Open the case and walk the board
steps.description: The Asset & Build Sheet has one row per part with its location, read from the part itself.
steps.where: The bench — case open, strap on
steps.instruction: Take the side panel off. Without removing anything, identify the board, the cooler, each memory slot, every drive and its connection, the supply, and every card.
steps.expectedOutput: The Asset & Build Sheet has one row per part with its location, read from the part itself.
instructionList: Photograph the open case before you touch anything; it is the "as found" picture.
Read the board model from the silk-screen print, usually between the slots.
Note which memory slots are filled and which are empty; the manual says which pairs belong together.
Read the supply rating from its label; a card added later must fit inside it.
Follow every cable from the drive to the board and name the interface: SATA, NVMe, USB header.

fixes.symptom: The CPU model is under the cooler and unreadable?
fixes.fix: Leave the cooler on. The live system reports it next step; the sticker is not the source anyway.

fixes.symptom: A screw will not come out?
fixes.fix: Stop. The wrong force strips the head. Ask before you drill anything.

steps.whatItMeans: A technician who can name every part by sight, and say where it plugs in, is halfway to every fault this machine will ever have.

steps.title: Prove the parts from the live system
steps.description: The board and the firmware report what is fitted. Paste the lines into the sheet.
steps.instruction: Boot the live stick and read the system, processor, memory and storage from the commands. Copy each model line into the sheet beside what you saw.

commands.cmd: sudo dmidecode -t system -t baseboard | grep -E "Manufacturer|Product Name|Serial"
commands.explain: The maker, the model and the serial, as the firmware stores them.
commands.sample:
Manufacturer: Dell Inc.
	Product Name: OptiPlex 7050
	Serial Number: 7XQ2R52
	Manufacturer: Dell Inc.
	Product Name: 0NW6H5

commands.explain: The processor by name, its cores and threads.
commands.sample:
CPU(s):                               4
Model name:                           Intel(R) Core(TM) i5-7500 CPU @ 3.40GHz
Thread(s) per core:                   1

commands.cmd: sudo dmidecode -t memory | grep -E "Size|Locator|Speed" | grep -v "No Module"
commands.explain: Every memory slot, what is in it and its speed. Empty slots say No Module Installed.
commands.sample:
Size: 8 GB
	Locator: DIMM1
	Speed: 2400 MT/s
	Size: 8 GB
	Locator: DIMM3
	Speed: 2400 MT/s

commands.explain: Every drive with its size, model and how it connects.
commands.sample:
NAME   SIZE TYPE MODEL                TRAN
sda  465.8G disk ST500DM002-1BD142    sata
sdb   28.9G disk USB DISK 3.0         usb

steps.whatItMeans: The sticker says what was sold. The firmware says what is fitted now. The sheet records the second.
steps.expectedOutput:
$ sudo dmidecode -t system | grep -E "Manufacturer|Product Name|Serial"
	Manufacturer: Dell Inc.
	Product Name: OptiPlex 7050
	Serial Number: 7XQ2R52

$ lscpu | grep "Model name"
Model name:                           Intel(R) Core(TM) i5-7500 CPU @ 3.40GHz

$ lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,TYPE,MODEL,TRAN
NAME   SIZE TYPE MODEL                TRAN
sda  465.8G disk ST500DM002-1BD142    sata

outputHighlights.label: The model the firmware knows. Yours differs; the line is what matters.
How the drive connects. This decides which spare you can fit.

steps.title: Read the disk health before you trust it
steps.description: SMART says whether the drive is failing. A failing drive is imaged first and replaced, never built on.
steps.instruction: Run the SMART health check on the PC disk and read the overall result and the reallocated sector count. Record both in the sheet.

commands.explain: The one-line verdict. PASSED or FAILED.
commands.sample: SMART overall-health self-assessment test result: PASSED

commands.explain: The three counters that predict failure: remapped sectors, hours, and sectors waiting to be remapped.
commands.sample:
5 Reallocated_Sector_Ct   0x0033   100   100   036    Pre-fail  Always       -       0
  9 Power_On_Hours          0x0032   083   083   000    Old_age   Always       -       15214
197 Current_Pending_Sector  0x0012   100   100   000    Old_age   Always       -       0

steps.whatItMeans: A drive with pending sectors can pass today and fail during the Week 2 install. Knowing now decides whether the spare goes in first.
steps.expectedOutput:
$ sudo smartctl -H /dev/sda
SMART overall-health self-assessment test result: PASSED

$ sudo smartctl -A /dev/sda | grep -E "Reallocated_Sector|Power_On_Hours"
  5 Reallocated_Sector_Ct   0x0033   100   100   036    Pre-fail  Always       -       0
  9 Power_On_Hours          0x0032   083   083   000    Old_age   Always       -       15214

fixes.symptom: smartctl says the device lacks SMART capability?
fixes.fix: It is behind a USB bridge or a RAID chip. Try `-d sat` after the command, or read it from a SATA port directly.

fixes.symptom: FAILED, or Current_Pending above zero?
fixes.fix: Image it today, in Week 2 order, then fit the spare drive. Record the decision in the sheet as a part replaced.

tasks.title: Work the fault with the six-step method
tasks.objective: The machine arrived with a fault. Find it the way the method says: one theory, one change, one result per row, failures kept.
prerequisites: The Asset & Build Sheet, so you know what is fitted
The vendor manual for the beep and LED codes
definitionOfDone: The symptom is written exactly, before any theory
Every attempt is a row: theory, the one change, the result
At least one theory was wrong and the row says so
The fix is verified with the machine reaching the firmware screen or the live USB

steps.title: Identify the problem: write the symptom exactly
steps.description: The log opens with an exact symptom and the code looked up for this model, and no theory yet.
steps.instruction: Power it on and write down exactly what it does: fans, lights, beeps, screen, and when it stops. Look the code up for this model.
steps.expectedOutput: The log opens with an exact symptom and the code looked up for this model, and no theory yet.
instructionList: Step 1 of the method: identify the problem. Observe, question, note what changed. No theory yet.
Count beeps and watch LED colours and blink patterns; write the pattern, not the feeling.
Look the pattern up in the vendor manual for this model. Different models reuse codes differently.
Back up before you touch anything that holds data: the image comes next week, so this week change hardware only.
steps.whatItMeans: The method starts with a symptom written down, because the first theory is wrong half the time and nobody remembers the symptom after three changes.

steps.title: Establish a theory, test it, one change at a time
steps.description: Each row has one theory, one change and one result, and the log keeps the rows that did not work.
steps.where: The bench — case open, strap on
steps.instruction: Write one theory from the symptom and the code. Change exactly one thing to test it and record the result. A wrong theory gets the next row.
steps.expectedOutput: Each row has one theory, one change and one result, and the log keeps the rows that did not work.
steps.danger: Unplug from the wall before the case opens. Never force a connector; a bent CPU pin is not a repair.
instructionList: Steps 2 and 3: a theory, then a test. Start with seating, cables and the supply switch.
One change per row. Reseat one module, swap one cable, pull one card.
Stuck? Minimum boot: board, CPU, one memory module, nothing else. Add parts back one at a time.
Memory suspected? Boot MemTest86+ from the live stick menu and let it run one full pass.
Step 4: once the theory holds, plan the fix and its rollback before you make it.

fixes.symptom: No power at all, no fan twitch?
fixes.fix: The supply, the wall lead, or the front-panel header. Test the supply with the paper-clip test or a known-good unit before blaming the board.

fixes.symptom: Fans spin, no video, no beeps?
fixes.fix: Memory or the video path. Minimum boot with one module; try the other module alone; try the onboard video with the card removed.

fixes.symptom: It posts but will not find a disk?
fixes.fix: The SATA cable and the power lead to the drive, then the SATA port in firmware setup. The SMART check already told you if the drive is dying.

steps.whatItMeans: Changing three things at once fixes the machine and teaches nothing. The row that says no change is the method doing its job.

steps.title: Verify the fix and document it
steps.description: The machine reaches the live USB, and the log records what it was and what to do if it returns.
steps.instruction: Steps 5 and 6: boot the live stick and read the memory and the drive back, then write what it was, the fix, and the prevention.

commands.explain: All the memory you fitted is seen. A module that is seated but dead shows as missing here.
commands.sample:
total        used        free      shared  buff/cache   available
Mem:            15Gi       1.2Gi        13Gi       180Mi       1.1Gi        14Gi

commands.explain: The disk is back and reports its size and model.
commands.sample:
NAME   SIZE MODEL
sda  465.8G ST500DM002-1BD142
sdb   28.9G USB DISK 3.0

commands.explain: The kernel log for anything still complaining. Empty is the good answer.
commands.sample: (no output: nothing is complaining)

steps.whatItMeans: A fix is proved by the thing that was broken working, read from the machine, and written so the next technician knows what to try first.
steps.expectedOutput:
$ free -h
               total        used        free      shared  buff/cache   available
Mem:            15Gi       1.2Gi        13Gi       180Mi       1.1Gi        14Gi

$ lsblk -d -o NAME,SIZE,MODEL
NAME   SIZE MODEL
sda  465.8G ST500DM002-1BD142

outputHighlights.label: The total should match the modules you fitted. 16 GB fitted reads as about 15Gi.

tasks.title: Set the firmware baseline
tasks.objective: Record the firmware version, set boot mode, boot order, Secure Boot and the setup password, and write every change down.
definitionOfDone: The firmware version on arrival and after any update are recorded
Boot mode is UEFI, Secure Boot is on, the TPM is enabled
Boot order is the internal disk first, USB second
Every setting changed is a row with its menu path

steps.title: Read the firmware version and the TPM state
steps.description: The version decides whether an update is due; the TPM decides whether Week 4 encryption is possible.
steps.instruction: Read the firmware version and date, and whether a TPM is present, from the live system. Record both before you change any setting.

commands.explain: The firmware maker, version and date. Compare the date with the vendor support page.
commands.sample:
Vendor: Dell Inc.
	Version: 1.29.0
	Release Date: 06/24/2024

commands.explain: A tpm0 entry and a 2 mean a TPM 2.0 is present and enabled.
commands.sample:
tpm0
2

steps.whatItMeans: Firmware older than the last security fix is a fault the sheet must name. No TPM means Week 4 encryption needs a different plan.
steps.expectedOutput:
$ sudo dmidecode -t bios | grep -E "Vendor|Version|Release Date"
	Vendor: Dell Inc.
	Version: 1.29.0
	Release Date: 06/24/2024

$ ls /sys/class/tpm/ && cat /sys/class/tpm/tpm0/tpm_version_major
tpm0
2

fixes.symptom: No tpm0 directory?
fixes.fix: Enter firmware setup and enable the TPM or PTT under Security. If the board has none, record it: Week 4 uses a password-only plan.

steps.title: Set the baseline in firmware setup
steps.description: Every setting is set, every change is a row with its menu path, and the setup password is recorded for the…
steps.where: The PC — firmware setup at power on
steps.instruction: Enter setup. Set UEFI boot, Secure Boot on, the TPM enabled, the internal disk first, and a setup password. Update the firmware if a newer version exists.
steps.expectedOutput: Every setting is set, every change is a row with its menu path, and the setup password is recorded for the team only.
steps.danger: A firmware update that loses power half-way can brick the board. Only update on mains power, and never interrupt it.
instructionList: Write the menu path for each setting as you change it; the next technician needs the path, not the idea.
Secure Boot on may stop the live stick booting; turn it off only when a step says so.
A setup password stops a passer-by changing the boot order. Record it in the sheet, nowhere else.
If you update the firmware, record the version before and after.
steps.whatItMeans: The firmware baseline is the first security control on the machine, and the one most technicians never write down.

tasks.title: Image the disk before anything changes
tasks.objective: Take a full image of the disk as it arrived, hash it, and record it before the installer touches the drive.
prerequisites: The IMAGES drive with free space of twice the disk
The disk health read in Week 1
definitionOfDone: A full disk image of the as-received state exists on the IMAGES drive
The image is hashed and the hash is in the register
The register says what was imaged, when, by whom and where it lives

steps.title: Take the as-received image with Clonezilla
steps.description: Clonezilla reports the image saved with every partition listed, and the folder exists on the IMAGES drive.
steps.where: The PC — booted from the Clonezilla stick
steps.instruction: Boot Clonezilla, choose device-image, pick the IMAGES drive as the home, choose savedisk, name the image as-received-<date>, and let it run. Do not pick the IMAGES drive as the source.
steps.expectedOutput: Clonezilla reports the image saved with every partition listed, and the folder exists on the IMAGES drive.
steps.danger: Source and destination are easy to swap in Clonezilla. Read the disk sizes twice; the source is the PC disk, the destination is IMAGES.
instructionList: device-image, then local_dev, then pick the IMAGES partition as /home/partimag.
Beginner mode, savedisk, name it as-received-YYYYMMDD, source is the internal disk.
Accept the defaults for compression and checking; let it check the image when it finishes.
Write the image name, the source disk and the start and end time in the register.

fixes.symptom: Clonezilla cannot see the IMAGES drive?
fixes.fix: It is NTFS and was not cleanly unmounted. Plug it into Windows, eject it properly, and try again.

fixes.symptom: It refuses a disk with pending sectors?
fixes.fix: Choose rescue mode when offered; the image is still worth taking. Record the sectors skipped.

steps.whatItMeans: The image is the way back. Everything from here on can be undone in one restore, and in Week 2 you prove it.

steps.title: Hash the image and record it
steps.description: An image without a hash cannot be shown to be the same image later.
steps.instruction: Boot the live stick, list the image folder and hash its parts. Put the hash of the partition image into the register and into the custody log.

commands.explain: The parts of a Clonezilla image. A file of a few bytes means it saved nothing.
commands.sample:
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root  12G Oct 26 10:41 sda2.ntfs-ptcl-img.gz.aa
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root  137 Oct 26 10:12 parts
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root   81 Oct 26 10:12 disk

commands.explain: The digest of the main partition image. This line goes in the register and the custody log.
commands.sample: 4d7a9c…e21f  /media/user/IMAGES/as-received-20261026/sda2.ntfs-ptcl-img.gz.aa

steps.whatItMeans: The hash is what lets Week 4 say the image you restore is the image you took. It takes a minute and settles every later argument.
steps.expectedOutput:
$ ls -lh /media/$USER/IMAGES/as-received-20261026/
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root  12G Oct 26 10:41 sda2.ntfs-ptcl-img.gz.aa
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root  137 Oct 26 10:12 parts

$ sha256sum /media/$USER/IMAGES/as-received-20261026/sda2.ntfs-ptcl-img.gz.aa
4d7a9c…e21f  /media/user/IMAGES/as-received-20261026/sda2.ntfs-ptcl-img.gz.aa

tasks.title: Install Windows and set the baseline
tasks.objective: Install Windows clean, add the drivers and updates, create the accounts, and record the baseline the machine now has.
definitionOfDone: Windows is installed on the internal disk with the edition and build recorded
No device in Device Manager carries a warning
Updates are current and the machine has rebooted after them
A named administrator and a standard user exist; the built-in Administrator is disabled

steps.title: Install Windows clean onto the internal disk
steps.description: Windows reaches the desktop from the internal disk, with the hostname you set and your named local administ…
steps.where: The PC — booted from the INSTALL stick
steps.instruction: Boot the INSTALL stick, choose a custom install, delete every partition on the internal disk, and install to the free space. Name the machine and your admin account.
steps.expectedOutput: Windows reaches the desktop from the internal disk, with the hostname you set and your named local administrator.
steps.danger: Deleting partitions is the point of no return. The IMAGES drive must be unplugged before the installer runs, so it cannot be chosen by mistake.
instructionList: Unplug IMAGES. The installer lists disks by size; a wrong click wipes the images.
Custom install, delete every partition on the internal disk, select the unallocated space.
Skip the Microsoft account where the installer allows a local one; this is a bench machine.
Hostname BENCH-T<team>; administrator named after you, not "admin".

fixes.symptom: The installer cannot find any disk?
fixes.fix: The storage controller is in RAID or VMD mode. Switch it to AHCI in firmware setup and record the change.

fixes.symptom: "This PC can't run Windows 11"?
fixes.fix: TPM or Secure Boot is off. Go back to the Week 1 baseline and check both; the sheet says what you set.

steps.whatItMeans: A clean install from checked media is the only way to know what is on the machine. An upgrade keeps whatever the last owner left.

steps.title: Drivers, updates and the reboot
steps.description: Every device recognised, every update applied, and the machine rebooted so the baseline is real.
steps.instruction: Install the chipset, network and graphics drivers from the vendor support site, run Windows Update until it finds nothing, reboot, then read the build and the device state back.

commands.cmd: Get-PnpDevice -Status Error | Select-Object Status, Class, FriendlyName
commands.explain: Devices Windows could not start. Empty is the goal; each row is a driver still to fetch.
commands.sample:
Status Class FriendlyName
------ ----- ------------

commands.cmd: systeminfo | findstr /C:"OS Name" /C:"OS Version" /C:"System Boot Time"
commands.explain: The edition, the build and the last reboot. The boot time proves the reboot after updates happened.
commands.sample:
OS Name:                   Microsoft Windows 11 Pro
OS Version:                10.0.26100 N/A Build 26100
System Boot Time:          26/10/2026, 14:02:11

commands.cmd: Get-HotFix | Sort-Object InstalledOn -Descending | Select-Object -First 3 HotFixID, InstalledOn
commands.explain: The latest updates applied, newest first. The dates should be this week.

steps.whatItMeans: A device with a warning is a fault the user will report in Week 3. An unpatched machine fails the first security check in Week 4.
steps.expectedOutput:
PS C:\> Get-PnpDevice -Status Error | Select-Object Status, Class, FriendlyName

tasks.title: Prove the image restores
tasks.objective: Take the post-install image, then restore the as-received image over it and time the restore, so both images are known to work.
learn: Why an untested backup is not a backup
definitionOfDone: A post-install image exists, hashed, in the register
The as-received image was restored and the machine booted from it
The restore time is two clock readings in the register
The post-install image was restored back and Windows is as baselined

steps.title: Take the post-install image
steps.description: The register has two images, each with a hash: as-received and post-install.
steps.where: The PC — booted from the Clonezilla stick
steps.instruction: Shut Windows down fully, plug IMAGES back in, boot Clonezilla and save a second image named post-install-<date>. Hash it from the live stick as before and record it.
steps.expectedOutput: The register has two images, each with a hash: as-received and post-install.
instructionList: A full shutdown, not fast startup: hold Shift when you click Shut down, or the disk is left dirty.
Same Clonezilla path as the first image; the name is the only difference.
Hash the partition image from the live stick and put the hash in the register.
steps.whatItMeans: Two images, two known states. Everything in Weeks 3 and 4 can be undone to either one.

steps.title: Restore the as-received image and time it
steps.description: The old system is back on the disk, and the register holds the start and end time of the restore.
steps.where: The PC — booted from the Clonezilla stick
steps.instruction: Read the clock. Restore as-received over the internal disk, boot it, and read the clock again when the old system reaches its sign-in screen.
steps.expectedOutput: The old system is back on the disk, and the register holds the start and end time of the restore.
steps.danger: restoredisk overwrites the whole internal disk. It is the point of this step, but read the target disk size twice.
instructionList: Write the start time before you press Enter on the restore.
restoredisk, choose as-received-<date>, target is the internal disk.
The end time is when the restored system answers, not when Clonezilla says done.
Record both times and the difference as the measured restore time.

fixes.symptom: The restored system will not boot, "no bootable device"?
fixes.fix: The boot mode changed since the image was taken. The old system was legacy; switch firmware to legacy for this boot and record it, then back to UEFI for the post-install restore.

steps.whatItMeans: A backup is a promise until it has been restored. The time is the number a manager asks for, and only a measured one is worth saying.

tasks.title: Connect it and prove the link

The address, gateway and DNS server are recorded
A name resolves and the gateway answers a ping

steps.title: Cable it and read the address

steps.instruction: Plug the PC into the bench switch and watch for the link light. Read the adapter speed, the address, the gateway and the DNS server, and record them.

commands.explain: The adapter is Up and the speed is what the switch port offers. 10 Mbps on a gigabit port means a bad cable.

Name     Status LinkSpeed
----     ------ ---------

DHCP Enabled. . . . . . . . . . . : Yes
   IPv4 Address. . . . . . . . . . . : 10.10.50.23(Preferred)
   Default Gateway . . . . . . . . . : 10.10.50.1
   DNS Servers . . . . . . . . . . . : 10.10.0.10

steps.whatItMeans: Every network fault in Week 3 is one of these four numbers being wrong. Knowing the right ones is how you spot the wrong one.

----     ------ ---------

fixes.symptom: Status Disconnected?
fixes.fix: The cable, then the other end. Swap the cable before anything else; it is the cheapest part and the usual fault.

fixes.symptom: An address starting 169.254?
fixes.fix: No DHCP answer reached the machine. Check the switch port is live and the server is reachable from another PC.

steps.title: Prove the path: gateway, name, outside
steps.description: Three tests, in order, so a failure says which hop is broken.
steps.instruction: Ping the gateway, resolve a name, then trace the route outside. Record the output; it is the known-good picture a Week 3 ticket is compared against.

commands.explain: The gateway answers, so the local segment works. Substitute your own gateway from the step before.
commands.sample:
Reply from 10.10.50.1: bytes=32 time<1ms TTL=64
Reply from 10.10.50.1: bytes=32 time<1ms TTL=64

commands.explain: The DNS server turns a name into an address. No answer here is a DNS fault, not a network one.
commands.sample:
Server:  dns.lab
Address:  10.10.0.10

Non-authoritative answer:
Name:    example.com
Addresses:  93.184.215.14

commands.explain: The first six hops out. Where the stars start is where the path breaks.
commands.sample:
Tracing route to 93.184.215.14 over a maximum of 6 hops

  2     2 ms     1 ms     1 ms  10.10.0.1
  3     9 ms     8 ms     9 ms  203.0.113.1

steps.whatItMeans: Gateway, name, route: the three questions in order. A technician who asks them in order never spends an hour on the wrong hop.

Reply from 10.10.50.1: bytes=32 time<1ms TTL=64

PS C:\> nslookup example.com
Non-authoritative answer:
Name:    example.com
Addresses:  93.184.215.14

PS C:\> tracert -d -h 6 example.com
  1    <1 ms    <1 ms    <1 ms  10.10.50.1

A printer prints a test page from bench.user

steps.description: A test page is printed from bench.user, both displays show the desktop, and the setup ticket records the pr…

fixes.fix: Cable, then input source on the display, then Detect in Settings. Three checks, in that order.

steps.whatItMeans: Printers and displays are most of a help desk's day. Doing it once as the user shows what the user sees.

steps.where: A teammate's machine, then the PC

tasks.title: Work three tickets with the method
tasks.objective: Another team breaks three things on the machine. Work each as a ticket, with the six steps shown, and close it with proof.
prerequisites: The known-good network picture from the connect task
The post-install image, in case a fault goes wrong
definitionOfDone: Three tickets, each with symptom, theory, test, fix and verification
Each ticket names the user, the time opened and the time closed
At least one ticket was escalated or needed a second theory

steps.title: Receive the faults and open the tickets
steps.description: Three tickets are open, each with the user's description and the time, and none has a theory yet.
steps.where: The bench — the other team hands over

steps.expectedOutput: Three tickets are open, each with the user's description and the time, and none has a theory yet.
instructionList: Suggested faults: a wrong DNS server, a loosened module or boot order, a stopped service or a removed printer.

deliverables.purpose: The six-step method as a record: identify the problem, establish a theory, test it, plan and act, verify, document. One row per attempt, including the ones that changed nothing, because ruling a theory out is the method working.

Step 4, plan the fix and its way back. Step 5, make it and verify full function.

DOMAINS.label: Technical capability
DOMAINS.definition: Skills, tools, commands and exam domains proven by pasted output that held every expected token.
DOMAINS.asks: Can this member operate the tools and run the commands the job needs?
DOMAINS.evidence: A verification record per step: the output hash, the tokens matched, the attempts, and a receipt in cloud mode.

DOMAINS.label: Professional execution
DOMAINS.definition: Procedures followed to standard, steps in order, first pastes, evidence named, checks met, documents controlled, work on time.
DOMAINS.asks: Does this member follow the runbook as written and deliver on the calendar?
DOMAINS.evidence: The order of verification stamps, the attempts, the file names, the Definition-of-Done checks, the control block and the cohort due dates.

DOMAINS.label: Problem solving
DOMAINS.definition: Faults logged and resolved, steps verified after a failed paste, stuck flags cleared, and the minutes from first paste to proof.
DOMAINS.asks: When something breaks, does this member find and fix it, and how long does it take?
DOMAINS.evidence: Fault, incident and triage rows with their outcome column, retries that verified, the append-only flag history and two stamps per step.

DOMAINS.label: Thought process
DOMAINS.definition: Decisions recorded against at least three options with rationale, rejected options, risk and rollback, and reasons written on change rows.
DOMAINS.asks: Does this member weigh options, say why, and plan the way back?
DOMAINS.evidence: Decision blocks with the option chosen, who chose it and when, the answers to the supporting questions, and the form lifecycle.

DOMAINS.label: Architecture and design
DOMAINS.definition: Design briefs, topologies, IP plans, bills of materials, decision records and as-built documents drafted, approved and issued.
DOMAINS.asks: Can this member design a system and write it down so another team can build it?
DOMAINS.evidence: The architecture and configuration forms of the role: rows filled, checks met, approved or issued, with the decisions on them.

DOMAINS.label: Team and communication
DOMAINS.definition: Hand-offs closed, RACI respected, peer reviews given, steps ticked for teammates, reports filed, notes written, handovers issued.
DOMAINS.asks: Does this member hand work on cleanly, review others and hold their lane?
DOMAINS.evidence: The lifecycle rows with who moved what, the hand-offs and their forms, the peer review queue, the reports and the notes.

DOMAINS.label: Learning and retention
DOMAINS.definition: Skills proved on a second task, verified again a week or more later, reused in another course, and the pace month on month.
DOMAINS.asks: Is this member still learning, and keeping what was learned?
DOMAINS.evidence: The verification stamps of every skill: first and last, the tasks and courses between them, and the last two months of them.

DOMAINS.label: Professional readiness
DOMAINS.definition: The tier per record item at ten verified uses, the exam weight verified, the work-role coverage and the readiness score.
DOMAINS.asks: Can this member consistently perform at a professional level in a real work environment?
DOMAINS.evidence: Every category of the record with its verified uses across courses, the published exam weights and the work roles’ required competencies.

KPIS.label: Skills verified
KPIS.numerator: Skills with at least one step verified from pasted output.
KPIS.denominator: Skills the role practises that carry a verifiable step.
KPIS.whyMember: Each verified skill names a task where the pasted output held every expected token.
KPIS.whyCompany: Skills backed by matched output rather than a tick, with the task behind each one named.

KPIS.label: Exam weight verified
KPIS.numerator: The published exam weight of every domain with a verified step, summed.
KPIS.denominator: The published exam weight of every domain the role practises, summed.
KPIS.whyMember: Shows which share of the exam blueprint the verified work already touches.
KPIS.whyCompany: Reads the verified work against the published exam domains and their weights.

KPIS.label: Commands verified
KPIS.numerator: Verified required steps that run a command.
KPIS.denominator: Verifiable required steps that run a command.
KPIS.whyMember: Command steps proven by their output; the table below splits them by tool.
KPIS.whyCompany: Tool use proven by output, per command step, split by tool in the table.

KPIS.label: Procedures to standard
KPIS.numerator: Followed procedures whose form cites a control code and was approved or issued.
KPIS.denominator: Procedures followed: every check due met and document control complete.
KPIS.whyMember: A runbook followed to a named control and approved by the team; a team fact.
KPIS.whyCompany: Procedures run to a cited NIST, ISO or SOC 2 control and approved by the team.

KPIS.label: Faults resolved
KPIS.numerator: Fault, incident and triage rows whose outcome column reads resolved.
KPIS.denominator: Fault, incident and triage rows the team filled on the forms of the role.
KPIS.whyMember: Every fault the team logged, and how many ended resolved; a team fact.
KPIS.whyCompany: Troubleshooting success read from the fault and incident records the team kept.

KPIS.label: Verified after retry
KPIS.numerator: Verified steps that took more than one paste.
KPIS.denominator: Verified steps.
KPIS.whyMember: A step that failed once and was then proven: the fault was found and fixed.
KPIS.whyCompany: How often a failed first paste was followed by a verified fix.

KPIS.label: Stuck flags cleared
KPIS.numerator: Stuck flags the member raised and later cleared.
KPIS.denominator: Stuck flags the member raised.
KPIS.whyMember: Asking for help and then getting past it both count; a flag never cleared says so.
KPIS.whyCompany: Blockers raised and worked through, from the append-only flag history.

KPIS.label: Time to resolution
KPIS.numerator: The median minutes from the first paste to the verification, per verified step with both stamps.
KPIS.denominator: Verified steps with both stamps; the share within the hour is the percentage.
KPIS.whyMember: The median, so one long gap moves nothing; a step left over a day is counted apart.
KPIS.whyCompany: Minutes from first attempt to proof, read from two recorded stamps, never a clock.

KPIS.label: Steps verified in order
KPIS.numerator: Tasks whose verifiable steps were verified in the authored order.
KPIS.denominator: Tasks with two or more verification records, so an order exists.
KPIS.whyMember: The procedure was run as written, step after step.
KPIS.whyCompany: Runbooks followed in order, read from the sequence of verification records.

KPIS.label: First-try verifications
KPIS.numerator: Verified steps whose first paste held every expected token.
KPIS.denominator: Verified steps.
KPIS.whyMember: Shown beside retries: a step verified after several pastes counts for as much.
KPIS.whyCompany: How often the first paste matched, printed beside how often it took more than one.

KPIS.label: Files named to convention
KPIS.numerator: Hashed files named to the evidence convention.
KPIS.denominator: Hashed files.
KPIS.whyMember: Evidence an auditor can find: date, team, tool and subject in every file name.
KPIS.whyCompany: Chain-of-custody hygiene: hashed files that follow the naming convention.

KPIS.label: Definition-of-Done met
KPIS.numerator: Definition-of-Done checks met on the forms of the role.
KPIS.denominator: Checks due on those forms through the current week.
KPIS.whyMember: Every check a form must pass this week, met or not, counted for the team.
KPIS.whyCompany: Work products measured against their own acceptance checks, week by week.

KPIS.label: Decisions recorded
KPIS.numerator: Decision blocks with an option chosen by this member.
KPIS.denominator: Decision blocks on the forms of the role, each with at least three options.
KPIS.whyMember: Each decision names the options weighed, the one chosen, who chose and when.
KPIS.whyCompany: Component, configuration and architecture choices made against named alternatives.

KPIS.label: Decisions justified
KPIS.numerator: Recorded decisions with every required supporting question answered.
KPIS.denominator: Decisions recorded by this member.
KPIS.whyMember: A choice with its reason, the rejected options and the risk accepted.
KPIS.whyCompany: Judgment shown in writing: rationale, rejected options, risk and rollback per decision.

KPIS.label: Decisions approved
KPIS.numerator: Recorded decisions on a form the team approved or issued.
KPIS.denominator: Decisions recorded by this member.
KPIS.whyMember: The team stood behind the choice; a team fact.
KPIS.whyCompany: Decisions that passed the team’s review and were issued.

KPIS.label: Changes with rollback
KPIS.numerator: Change-record rows with a rollback or back-out written.
KPIS.denominator: Change-record rows on the forms of the role.
KPIS.whyMember: Every change the team logged, and how many had a way back written down first.
KPIS.whyCompany: Change discipline: a rollback plan on every recorded change.

KPIS.label: Hand-offs completed
KPIS.numerator: Hand-offs whose named deliverable reached approved or issued.
KPIS.denominator: Hand-offs of the tasks of the role.
KPIS.whyMember: Work handed to another role that the team then approved or issued.
KPIS.whyCompany: Cross-role hand-offs closed by an approved document.

KPIS.label: RACI respected
KPIS.numerator: Lifecycle moves the member made in the role the RACI names for that move.
KPIS.denominator: Lifecycle moves the member made on forms with a RACI.
KPIS.whyMember: Submitting as the drafter, approving as the approver: the lane was held.
KPIS.whyCompany: Role discipline on documents, read from who moved what.

KPIS.label: Peer reviews given
KPIS.numerator: Blind peer reviews the member completed.
KPIS.denominator: Peer reviews assigned to the member.
KPIS.whyMember: Reviews of other teams’ frozen work, answered question by question.
KPIS.whyCompany: Review work done for others, from the blind review queue.

KPIS.label: Teammate steps ticked
KPIS.numerator: Required steps the member ticked on another role’s tasks.
KPIS.denominator: No denominator: a count.
KPIS.whyMember: Steps done on a teammate’s task, so a lane short of hands still finished.
KPIS.whyCompany: Help given across roles, counted in steps.

KPIS.label: On time
KPIS.numerator: Tasks whose last verification fell on or before the week due date.
KPIS.denominator: Tasks with a verification; needs the cohort start date.
KPIS.whyMember: The due date comes from the cohort calendar; without one the row says so.
KPIS.whyCompany: Reliability against a calendar, read from the verification stamps and the cohort start.

KPIS.label: Document control complete
KPIS.numerator: Forms with data whose document-control block is complete.
KPIS.denominator: Forms of the role with data.
KPIS.whyMember: Id, version, owner, date and status on every document the team filled.
KPIS.whyCompany: Document control kept on every filled form: id, version, owner, date, status.

KPIS.label: Controls cited
KPIS.numerator: Distinct control codes on approved or issued forms the role drafts.
KPIS.denominator: Distinct control codes the forms of the role cite.
KPIS.whyMember: The published controls the approved documents cite, by code.
KPIS.whyCompany: Control codes practised through approved documents, by standard.

KPIS.label: Instructor approved
KPIS.numerator: Forms of the role whose latest instructor review is approved.
KPIS.denominator: Forms of the role.
KPIS.whyMember: Forms an instructor reviewed and approved; the latest review per form counts.
KPIS.whyCompany: Forms with an instructor verdict of approved, the latest review per form.

KPIS.label: Skills proved twice
KPIS.numerator: Skills with verified steps on two or more distinct tasks.
KPIS.denominator: Skills with at least one verified step.
KPIS.whyMember: A skill verified on two different tasks was carried from one context to another.
KPIS.whyCompany: Verification repeated on a second task is harder to reach by luck or by copying.

KPIS.label: Skills retained
KPIS.numerator: Skills verified again seven or more days after their first verification.
KPIS.denominator: Skills with at least one verified step.
KPIS.whyMember: Proof a week or more apart: the skill stayed.
KPIS.whyCompany: Retention read from the gap between two verification stamps on the same skill.

KPIS.label: Learning velocity
KPIS.numerator: Verified steps in the twenty-eight days before the page clock.
KPIS.denominator: Verified steps in the twenty-eight days before those; the percentage caps at one hundred.
KPIS.whyMember: This month against last: rising, level or slowing, from the verification stamps.
KPIS.whyCompany: Pace of verified work, month on month, from recorded stamps.

KPIS.label: Profile coverage
KPIS.numerator: Required competencies of the selected work role or environment profile at verified or better.
KPIS.denominator: Required competencies the selected work role or environment profile names.
KPIS.whyMember: Measures the verified skills against a job role or a published company profile, with the untaught gap named.
KPIS.whyCompany: Coverage of the competencies a work role or an environment profile requires, read from verified steps.

STANDARDS.label: NIST CSF
STANDARDS.description: NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover
STANDARDS.why: Organises all security work into six functions. Tagging a step here shows which part of the lifecycle it strengthens and proves the work covered the whole picture, not just attack or defence.

STANDARDS.label: CIS
STANDARDS.description: CIS Critical Security Controls v8 and the CIS Benchmarks
STANDARDS.why: A prioritised "do these first" list of safeguards. A CIS tag means this step implements an industry-baseline control that auditors and blue teams recognise at once.

STANDARDS.label: NIST 800-61
STANDARDS.description: NIST SP 800-61 Computer Security Incident Handling Guide
STANDARDS.why: The incident-handling playbook: prepare, detect and analyse, contain, eradicate, recover, learn. This tag means the step is part of a defensible, court-ready incident response process.

STANDARDS.label: ISO 27001
STANDARDS.why: The certifiable information security management standard. This tag means the step produces the documented policy or evidence an ISO 27001 audit expects to see.

STANDARDS.label: ITIL 4
STANDARDS.description: ITIL 4 service management practices: change, incident, problem, release
STANDARDS.why: The operating disciplines a network team is judged on: change, incident and problem management. A tag here means the step is not just technically right but done the way an organisation can audit: requested, reviewed, reversible and recorded.

STANDARDS.label: NIST SP 800-53
STANDARDS.description: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 security and privacy controls
STANDARDS.why: The federal control catalogue the sixteen CISSP control statements are drawn from (PM-1, SC-7, AC-2). A tag here means the step writes or proves one of those controls.

STANDARDS.label: NIST SP 800-34
STANDARDS.description: NIST SP 800-34 Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems
STANDARDS.why: Where the business impact analysis and the recovery objectives (RTO, RPO) come from. A recovery plan that cites it states what must come back, and how fast.

STANDARDS.label: NIST SP 800-40
STANDARDS.description: NIST SP 800-40 Guide to Enterprise Patch Management Planning
STANDARDS.why: Patching as a managed routine rather than a scramble: inventory, prioritise, test, deploy, verify. A vulnerability management SOP that cites it has a defensible cadence.

STANDARDS.label: ISO/IEC 27037
STANDARDS.description: ISO/IEC 27037 identification, collection, acquisition and preservation of digital evidence
STANDARDS.why: How evidence is collected and kept so it still counts later: identify, collect, acquire, preserve, with a chain of custody. An evidence log that cites it can be trusted in a dispute.

CUSTODY_RULES: Preserve the original — work on copies; never edit or rename the original artifact after collection.
Name every artifact `YYYYMMDD_TeamXX_Tool_Action.ext` so it is dated, attributed and self-describing.
Hash on collection: `sha256sum <file> >> Evidence_Hashes.txt`. Verify on receipt/before reporting: `sha256sum -c Evidence_Hashes.txt`.
Log every artifact in this file the moment it is collected — and log every hand-off (who → who, when).
Keep every artifact for a week in `~/team-artifacts/week-N/`; the team package gathers them into `04_Testing_and_Findings/Evidence/`. Keep originals read-only and backed up.
One custodian holds the evidence at a time; record each transfer so the chain is unbroken.

ERROR_ROWS.fix: Add sudo in front on Linux (sudo <command>). On Windows/PowerShell, close it and reopen with “Run as administrator”.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: Connection refused / No route to host / host seems down
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: You can’t reach the target — it’s off, the IP is wrong, or you’re not on the right network.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: ping the address first. Confirm the machine is powered on and that you are on the same subnet as it

variants.then: , and that you set the right IP in Lab access.
variants.otherwise: — a host in another zone only answers once the route between them exists.

variants.then: For nmap, add -Pn to scan a host that blocks ping.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: You’re in the wrong folder, or the path/filename is wrong.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Run pwd to see where you are and cd ~ to go home.

variants.then: For hydra, rockyou is gzipped by default — unzip it once: sudo gunzip /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt.gz
variants.otherwise: Check the file really exists with ls before you edit it — a config path is easy to mistype.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: That’s a placeholder, not a real address — you copied it literally.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Open the Lab access panel at the top of the Tasks tab and enter {label}; the site then fills it into every command automatically.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: ssh: connect to host … Operation timed out (from home)
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: Your laptop is not on the tailnet, or the host is not.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Check the Tailscale client is signed in and connected on your laptop, then run tailscale status on the host — it must list the host as online. On campus you can still reach it on its 10.10.30.T address while you sort this out.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: The Proxmox console times out but SSH works
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The path is fine; the web service or the port is not.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Run systemctl status pveproxy --no-pager over SSH. Remember the console is on port 8006 and https, not http — a plain http:// URL simply hangs.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: It worked yesterday and not today
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The host rebooted and something did not come back, or your address changed.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: systemctl is-active tailscaled on the host must read active. The host keeps the same Tailscale address across reboots, so if the address you saved has changed, you are looking at a rebuilt host that was re-authorised as a new device.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: Permission denied (publickey) after setting up keys
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The key is not where the server expects it, or the account is wrong.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Run ssh -v to see which key is offered, and confirm you are connecting as the right user. Password login is still enabled until Week 4 hardens it, so you have a way back in — use it rather than locking yourself out further.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The VM cannot reach the Core over the ops network — the second NIC, the VLAN tag or the bridge is wrong.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: On the host, ip -br a must show vmbr9 UP with the team’s 10.20.T.1 address. Inside the VM, the second interface needs its 10.20.T.x address and no gateway. Still nothing: the switch port is not trunking VLAN 20 — the Networking deep-dive owns that.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: Some commands (a bare ping, a large download, a package install) run until you stop them, or they’re waiting on a slow or unreachable host.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Press Ctrl+C to stop it. Re-check reachability (ping), and give a genuinely long job a minute

variants.otherwise: — an OS install or a big apt upgrade takes minutes, not seconds.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: When anything fails, the error’s last line usually names the real problem.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Match that line to the rows above. Also double-check you’re on the machine the step’s WHERE chip names — running the right command on the wrong host is the most common cause.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Open a terminal
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: On a Linux desktop, click the black terminal icon or press Ctrl+Alt+T. On a server you reach over SSH, the terminal is the session itself. You type commands here and press Enter to run them.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: The prompt
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: A line ending in $ (or #) is the prompt — it means the terminal is waiting for you. You don’t type the $ itself.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Paste a command
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: Copy from this site, then in the terminal press Ctrl+Shift+V (plain Ctrl+V often does nothing in a terminal). Right-click → Paste also works.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Run one line at a time
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: When a step shows several numbered commands, run them one by one — paste one, press Enter, wait for it to finish, then the next.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: sudo = run as admin
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: sudo runs a command with admin rights (it may ask for your password — typing shows nothing, that’s normal). On Windows/PowerShell, instead right-click PowerShell → “Run as administrator”.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Stop a stuck command
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: Press Ctrl+C to cancel a command that hangs or runs forever (e.g. a ping with no -c limit).
